newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium frees former minister held in murder case.
newsitem.headline: Belgium frees former minister held in murder case.

text.p: A Belgian court on Thurday released former minister Alain Van der Biest, who was being held in connection with the 1991 murder of a prominent politician.
But the charges against him have not been dropped, his lawyer said.
"Mr. Van der Biest has been freed," a spokeswoman for the Liege court told Reuters.
Another official said he would be allowed to leave Lantin prison, near the eastern Belgian city of Liege, later on Thursday after completing release formalities.

Van der Biest, a former pensions minister in the Belgian federal government and interior affairs minister in the Walloon regional government, was arrested on September 8 last year and charged in connection with the murder of fellow socialist Andre Cools.
"The charges against my client were not dropped," Van der Biest's lawyer Jean-Luc Dessy told RTBF television, adding that he hoped the case would come to trial soon.

Van der Biest's former personal secretary Richard Taxquet and his former driver Pino Di Mauro remain in jail awaiting trial in connection with the murder, along with four Italians or Belgians of Italian origin.
In all, seven arrests have been made in Belgium since last summer in connection with the Cools murder. Van der Biest is the first person to be released from preventive detention.
In October Tunisian police arrested two Tunisian hitmen suspected of having gunned down Cools.
A member of the team investigating the murder told Reuters on Thursday the Tunisians had confessed to the contract killing but that they had not mentioned Van der Biest's name.
"Van der Biest's release only means that the court considered that there were not enough indications against him to continue his preventive detention, but he remains under investigation," he said.
Cools -- a former minister and the patriarch of socialist politics in the southern, Francophone half of Belgium -- was gunned down outside his mistress's home on July 18, 1991.
Five years later, the Belgian judiciary is still not sure who ordered his assassination.

But the investigation has led to the discovery of a series of corruption scandals, notably the arms-for-bribes Agusta army helicopter scandal, which has led to the resignation of four Belgian ministers and of former Belgian NATO Secretary General Willy Claes in 1994-95.
